scenes.title: The Name Problem
narration: Have you ever told a story and kept repeating the same name over and over?
Arjun went to school. Arjun ate lunch. Arjun played football.
It sounds a bit silly, doesn't it?

scenes.title: What are Pronouns
narration: Pronouns are special words that take the place of a noun.
Instead of saying the name again, we use words like he, she, or it.
These tiny words keep our sentences short, smooth, and easy to read.

scenes.title: Using Pronouns Correctly
narration: Let's fix our story. Arjun went to school.
He ate lunch and he played football.
See how much better it flows when we use he instead of Arjun?
If it were Priya, we would use she instead.

scenes.title: Summary and Practice
narration: Pronouns replace nouns to stop us from repeating names too often.
Common pronouns include I, you, he, she, it, we, and they.
Think about it: How would you describe your best friend using a pronoun today?

scenes.title: What Are Nouns?
narration: Look around your classroom, what do you see?
Everything you see has a special name.
These naming words are called nouns.

scenes.title: Types of Nouns
narration: Nouns can be a person like Rohan.
They can be a place like Delhi.
They can be a thing like a book.
They can even be animals like a tiger.

scenes.title: Spotting Nouns
narration: Let us look at a short sentence.
In this sentence, cat is a noun.
Fish is also a noun here.
Both words name things we know.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Nouns name people, places, and things.
They help us describe our world.
Can you name three nouns in your house?

scenes.title: What Are Action Words
narration: Have you ever noticed how busy your school playground is during recess?
Children run, jump, and laugh while playing games together.
These words that show action are called verbs.

scenes.title: Spotting The Verb
narration: A verb is the engine of your sentence, making things happen.
Without a verb, your sentence would just stand still.
Think of a verb as what the subject does.
If you can do it, it is likely a verb.

scenes.title: A Day With Rohan
narration: Let us look at Rohan eating his breakfast at home.
Rohan eats his delicious poha with a spoon.
Then, Rohan kicks his football in the park.
Finally, he sleeps soundly in his bed.

scenes.title: Quick Verb Recap
narration: Verbs are words that show actions like jumping, reading, or playing.
Every complete sentence needs at least one verb to work.
Can you find the verb in this sentence: Ravi writes a letter?

scenes.title: Spotting Objects at Home
narration: Have you ever lost your cricket ball in your messy room?
To find it, we need tiny words called prepositions.
They tell us exactly where something is hiding.

scenes.title: Understanding Preposition Rules
narration: A preposition sits before a noun to show a relationship.
Think of them as bridge words connecting places and objects.
Common ones are in, on, at, and under.

scenes.title: Finding Rohan's Cricket Ball
narration: Look, Rohan's ball is on the wooden chair.
Now it rolled in the blue basket.
Finally, it hides under the study table.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Prepositions link nouns to show their location.
They make our sentences clear and helpful.
Think about it: Where is your school bag right now?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Boring Sentences
narration: Have you ever read a sentence that felt a bit plain, like a dry roti?
Imagine saying, I have a bag. It tells us something, but it is not very exciting.
What if we added a special word to describe that bag?

scenes.title: Meet the Adjective
narration: An adjective is a describing word that tells us more about a noun.
It can tell us about size, like a big elephant.
It can tell us about color, like a green parrot.
It can even tell us about quality, like a yummy mango.

scenes.title: Using Adjectives in India
narration: Let us describe a busy market in Delhi.
We see a bright scarf, a loud shopkeeper, and a sweet jalebi.
Instead of just saying shop, we say crowded shop.
These words paint a colorful picture in our minds.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Adjectives are words that describe nouns by giving us extra details.
They help us explain how things look, feel, or taste.
Can you think of three adjectives to describe your favorite toy?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Action Words
narration: Imagine Rohan is running in the park.
But how does he run? Fast or slow?
Today we learn about special words that describe actions.

scenes.title: What is an Adverb?
narration: An adverb tells us more about a verb, like how an action happens.
Many adverbs end in the two letters L and Y.
They change a simple verb into a descriptive sentence.

scenes.title: Adverbs in Action
narration: Look at this sentence: Priya speaks softly.
Speaks is the verb and softly is the adverb.
Now try this: The bird sings loudly.
Loudly tells us how the bird is singing.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Adverbs describe verbs and often end in LY.
They make our writing exciting and clear.
Think about it: How would you describe how you eat your lunch?

scenes.title: The Magic Glue Words
narration: Have you ever wanted to join two short sentences into one big, smooth sentence?
Meet conjunctions, the special glue words that stick ideas together.
Without them, our speech would sound like short, choppy robot talk.

scenes.title: How Conjunctions Work
narration: The word and adds information to your sentence.
The word but shows a change or a difference.
The word or lets you choose between two things.

scenes.title: Let Us Practice Together
narration: Rohan likes cricket. Rohan likes football. We join these with and.
Rohan likes cricket and football becomes our new sentence.
I want a dosa, but the shop is closed today.
Would you like tea or milk for breakfast?

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Conjunctions connect words and ideas to make sentences flow better.
Remember, use and, but, and or to bridge your thoughts.
Think about it: can you write one sentence using two different conjunctions?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Little Words
narration: Have you ever wondered why we say an apple but a banana?
These tiny words are called articles.
They help us point to nouns like people, places, or things.

scenes.title: When to Use A and An
narration: Use a before words starting with a consonant sound, like a cat.
Use an before words starting with a vowel sound, like an egg.
Remember, the sound matters more than the letter itself.

scenes.title: Using The for Specific Things
narration: Use the when you are talking about one specific thing.
If you point to the Taj Mahal, use the.
It is the only one of its kind in India.

scenes.title: Quick Recap and Challenge
narration: Use a or an for any item, and the for something special.
You have learned how to use these three simple tools.
Think about it: would you say a umbrella or an umbrella?

scenes.title: The Surprise in Everyday Life
narration: Have you ever stubbed your toe and shouted Ouch?
Or maybe you saw a beautiful rainbow and yelled Wow!
These short, punchy words are called interjections.

scenes.title: How Interjections Work
narration: Interjections are words that show strong feelings.
They do not connect to other words in a sentence.
They stand all alone, usually with an exclamation mark.

scenes.title: Examples in Action
narration: When Arjun finds a lost coin, he shouts Hurray!
When Meera sees a scary spider, she says Eek!
When Priya is quiet in the library, she uses Shh.
Notice how each word stands apart from the rest.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Interjections show our big, loud emotions.
They always take an exclamation mark to show feeling.
Think about it: What interjection would you use if you won a cricket match?

scenes.title: The Daily Habit Hook
narration: Have you noticed how we talk about things we do every single day?
Look at Rohan. He brushes his teeth every morning.
Simple present tense helps us describe these regular habits and facts.

scenes.title: How to Build It
narration: For I, you, we, and they, we use the base verb.
I eat breakfast. They play in the park.
But wait! For he, she, or it, add an s at the end.
She walks to school. It rains in July.

scenes.title: Example in Action
narration: Let us see Priya in her kitchen.
Priya cooks yummy dal every day.
Because Priya is a she, we say cooks with an s.
If we say they, it becomes they cook.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember, use the base verb for most, but add s for he, she, and it.
Simple present is for habits, facts, and truths.
Think about it: what is one thing you do every day?

scenes.title: Spotting Action In The Park
narration: Have you noticed how we describe things happening right this second at the park?
Look at Rohan, he is kicking the football.
We use the present continuous tense for these ongoing actions.

scenes.title: Building The Present Continuous
narration: First, we need a helping verb like is, am, or are.
Then, we add the main verb with an ing ending.
Remember, the action must be happening right now.

scenes.title: Examples At The Market
narration: Amrita is buying fresh mangoes at the market.
The shopkeepers are shouting prices to the crowd.
I am eating a sweet jalebi while walking.

scenes.title: Recap And Think
narration: Use is, am, are plus a verb with ing.
It tells us what is happening at this very moment.
Think about it: what are you doing right this second?

scenes.title: What Happened Before
narration: Do you remember what you ate for breakfast this morning?
When we talk about things that finished, we use the simple past.
Let us explore how to change words to show they already happened.

scenes.title: Adding The Magic ED
narration: For many verbs, we simply add the letters E and D to the end.
The word jump becomes jumped when you played in the park.
The word cook becomes cooked when Rohan made yummy parathas.

scenes.title: Rahul at the Museum
narration: Rahul visited the museum yesterday to see old history.
He walked through the large stone halls.
He watched a movie about the great kings.
He learned many new things about his country.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Remember, simple past tells us about things that are already done.
Most times, we just add E D to the action word.
Think about it: what is the past form of the word play?

scenes.title: What Happened Already
narration: Have you ever wondered how to talk about things you just finished?
Meet Rohan who has just cleaned his room.
We use the present perfect to connect the past to now.

scenes.title: Building the Sentence
narration: To make this tense, we use have or has.
Use has for he, she, or it.
Use have for I, you, we, or they.
Then, add the past participle of the verb.

scenes.title: Rohan Eats Lunch
narration: Look at Rohan. He has eaten his lunch.
I have finished my homework for today.
They have played cricket in the park.

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Remember, use have or has plus the past action.
It shows something happened but still matters right now.
Think about it: What is one thing you have done today?

scenes.title: What Were You Doing?
narration: Imagine you were playing in the park yesterday when it suddenly started to rain.
We use the past continuous tense to describe actions that were happening at a specific time.
Have you ever wondered how to say what you were doing in the past?

scenes.title: Building the Sentence
narration: To make this tense, we start with the helper words was or were.
We use was for singular subjects like I, he, she, or it.
We use were for plural subjects like you, we, or they.
Then, we add the action word plus the letters i-n-g.

scenes.title: A Day in Delhi
narration: Let us look at Rohan in Delhi. He was eating a delicious samosa at noon.
At the same time, his friends were playing cricket near the India Gate.
Notice how we use was for Rohan and were for his friends.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, use was or were plus the ing action word.
This tells us about actions that were continuing in the past.
Think about it: What were you doing exactly one hour ago?

scenes.title: When Did It Happen
narration: Have you ever done something before another action happened in the past?
Meet Rohan who felt hungry after he had finished his homework.
We use the past perfect tense to show which action finished first.

scenes.title: Building The Sentence
narration: To make it, we use the word had plus the past participle.
The past participle is often the verb ending in ed.
For example, say he had played cricket yesterday.
Even if the subject is I, you, or they, we always use had.

scenes.title: A Story in Action
narration: Look at Sia who reached the bus stop.
But, the bus had left before she arrived.
The bus leaving is the first action, so we say it had left.
Sia arriving is the second action, written in simple past.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Use had plus the past participle for the earlier action.
It helps us sequence two events that both happened in the past.
Think about it: what had you done before you came to school today?

scenes.title: The Hook: Meet Rohan
narration: Look at Rohan eating a juicy mango in the park.
Have you ever wondered what makes a sentence complete?
Every sentence needs two special parts to work.

scenes.title: The Subject and Predicate
narration: The subject is the person or thing doing the action.
The predicate tells us what the subject is doing.
Together, they form a perfect, clear sentence.

scenes.title: An Example in Action
narration: Let us take the sentence: Priya reads books.
Priya is our subject because she is the person.
Reads books is our predicate, showing her action.
See how they link together to make sense?

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, the subject is who, and the predicate is what.
Every complete sentence must have both parts.
Can you find the subject in the sentence: Dogs bark?

scenes.title: A Look Into Tomorrow
narration: Look at your calendar, what will you do tomorrow?
When we talk about things not yet done, we use the future tense.
We often use the word will to show something is coming.

scenes.title: How We Build Sentences
narration: To make a future sentence, start with your subject.
Next, add the magic helper word will.
Finally, add the action word in its basic form.
It is that simple to talk about tomorrow.

scenes.title: An Example With Rohan
narration: Rohan is hungry for his favorite snack.
Rohan will eat an apple at four.
See how we use an before apple?
He will finish it quickly.

scenes.title: Recap And Think
narration: Use will plus the base verb for the future.
It helps us talk about plans and dreams.
Think about it, what will you do this weekend?

scenes.title: Spotting the Simple Sentence
narration: Have you ever wondered how we build a clear sentence when we talk or write?
A simple sentence is like a small block that tells one complete thought clearly.
Every simple sentence needs two main parts to make sense: a subject and a predicate.

scenes.title: The Subject and Predicate
narration: The subject tells us who or what the sentence is about, like Rohan.
The predicate tells us what the subject is doing, like eats a mango.
When we join them, we get a complete thought: Rohan eats a mango.

scenes.title: Building Our Example
narration: Let's build one together. Our subject is Priya.
Now, add an action, which is the verb. Priya runs.
Finally, we add details: Priya runs in the park.
See? It starts with a capital letter and ends with a period.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember, a simple sentence has a subject, a predicate, and one complete thought.
Always use a capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end.
Can you write a simple sentence about your favorite Indian festival today?

scenes.title: What Are You Doing Tomorrow?
narration: Have you ever thought about what you will be doing this time tomorrow?
Imagine it is Saturday and you have big plans with your friends.
We use the Future Continuous tense to talk about actions happening then.

scenes.title: Building The Tense
narration: To make this tense, we use the words will be plus the verb with ing.
For example, look at the word play.
It becomes will be playing to show a future action.

scenes.title: Rohan's Busy Saturday
narration: Let us see what Rohan is doing in Delhi this weekend.
At ten o'clock, he will be reading a book.
By noon, he will be eating delicious aloo parathas.
And at four, he will be playing cricket.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Remember, we use will be plus ing for actions continuing in the future.
It describes something that will be in progress at a specific time.
Think about it: What will you be doing this time next Sunday?

scenes.title: The Sentence Hook
narration: Have you ever tried to join two short sentences into one big, strong sentence?
Meet Rohan, who loves to eat mangoes and loves to play cricket.
Instead of saying them separately, we can link them together easily.

scenes.title: Using Conjunctions
narration: We use special connecting words called conjunctions to join two complete thoughts.
Think of the FANBOYS acronym to help you remember these special joining words.
When you join two full sentences, always place a comma before the conjunction.

scenes.title: Putting It Together
narration: Let's take Rohan eats a mango and Rohan plays cricket.
We add a comma and the word and to make it one sentence.
Now it reads: Rohan eats a mango, and he plays cricket.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, a compound sentence joins two complete thoughts with a comma and a conjunction.
Using these tools makes your writing flow much more smoothly.
Think about it: Can you write a compound sentence about your favorite Indian festival?

Sentence Structure: Active and Passive V.topic: Sentence Structure: Active and Passive Voice
Sentence Structure: Active and Passive V.title: Who Did It: Active vs Passive

scenes.title: The Mystery of the Action
narration: Have you ever wondered why we say things in different ways?
Let's watch Rohan eat a delicious mango.
We can say this in two different ways!

scenes.title: Learning the Active Voice
narration: First, the active voice puts the doer at the start.
Rohan ate the mango.
Rohan is the star because he does the action.
It is simple and clear to read.

scenes.title: The Passive Voice Swap
narration: Now, let us try the passive voice.
The mango was eaten by Rohan.
See how the mango moved to the front?
The action is now the main focus.

scenes.title: Quick Recap and Challenge
narration: Active means the doer goes first.
Passive means the object goes first.
Think about it: Can you write a sentence about your favorite toy in passive voice?

scenes.title: The Hook
narration: Have you ever tried to build a tall tower with blocks?
Sentences are just like those blocks, built from smaller pieces called clauses.
Do you know what makes a group of words a real sentence?

scenes.title: What is a Clause
narration: A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb.
The subject is who or what the sentence is about.
The verb tells us the action happening.
Every complete sentence needs at least one independent clause.

scenes.title: Example: Rohan Eats Mangoes
narration: Let us look at: Rohan eats sweet mangoes.
Rohan is our subject, the person doing the action.
Eats is our verb, the action he is doing.
Together, they form a complete thought that stands alone.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, a clause needs a subject and a verb to be complete.
If it stands alone, it is an independent clause.
Think about it: can you write a sentence with a subject and a verb today?

scenes.title: The Sentence Puzzle
narration: Have you ever heard someone say, He run fast? It sounds a bit funny, right?
A sentence is like a team where the subject and verb must match perfectly.
Today, we learn how to make our subjects and verbs agree like best friends.

scenes.title: Matching the Rules
narration: If the subject is singular, like Rohan or a cat, the verb needs an s.
Rohan eats a mango. See how the verb eats has that special s?
If the subject is plural, like they or the children, the verb stays plain.
They run to the park. No extra s needed here, just the base verb.

scenes.title: Practice With Me
narration: Let us try one. The dog barks at the postman. Is it correct?
Yes! Dog is one, so we add the s to the verb bark.
Now, the birds fly high. Birds is plural, so we use fly.
You did it! No s for plural, just the simple action word.

scenes.title: Remember the Rules
narration: Singular subjects love the letter s on their verb friends.
Plural subjects like their verbs plain and simple.
Think about it: Why does she sing sound better than she sing?

scenes.title: The Hook: Joining Ideas
narration: Have you ever wanted to tell a long story about your day in just one sentence?
Sometimes, short sentences feel like they are missing a little extra information.
Today we will learn how to build complex sentences using special joining words.

scenes.title: The Idea: How It Works
narration: A complex sentence combines one independent clause with one dependent clause.
An independent clause is a complete thought that stands on its own.
A dependent clause needs more information and starts with words like because, although, or since.

scenes.title: Example: Rohan's School Day
narration: Rohan played football, but he needed a reason to explain why he was tired.
We can say: Rohan was tired because he played football all afternoon.
See how because connects the main idea to the reason?
You could also say: Although he was tired, Rohan finished his homework.

scenes.title: Recap: Practice Makes Perfect
narration: Remember, a complex sentence uses a joining word to link two different ideas together.
Use words like since, because, and although to add detail to your writing.
Think about it: Can you write one complex sentence about your favorite meal in India?

Sentence Structure: Direct and Indirect.topic: Sentence Structure: Direct and Indirect Speech
Sentence Structure: Direct and Indirect.title: Reporting What People Say

scenes.title: The Daily Chat
narration: Have you ever told a friend what someone else said to you?
Meet Rohan, who says, I like mangoes.
We use quotation marks to show his exact words.

scenes.title: Changing the Words
narration: When we repeat it later, we change it to indirect speech.
We say, Rohan said that he liked mangoes.
Notice how the word like changes to liked.
The quotation marks disappear in indirect speech.

scenes.title: A Classroom Example
narration: Teacher Anjali says, I am happy today.
To report this, we say, Anjali said that she was happy.
We changed I to she, and am to was.

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Direct speech uses exact words and quotation marks.
Indirect speech reports the words using past tense.
Think about it: How would you report a friend saying, I am hungry?

scenes.title: A Curious Little Question
narration: Have you ever wondered how to turn a statement into a question?
We add a little tag at the end, like a tail!
Let's learn how Rohan uses these tags.

scenes.title: How to Build a Tag
narration: If the sentence is positive, the tag is negative.
For example, you say, Rohan is happy, isn't he?
If the sentence is negative, the tag becomes positive.
So, Rohan is not sad, is he?

scenes.title: Rohan at the Market
narration: Rohan is buying apples at the market today.
The statement is, They are fresh, aren't they?
He pays ten rupees, it wasn't expensive, was it?

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Remember, positive sentences need negative tags.
Negative sentences need positive tags.
Think about it: How would you tag, You are reading this?

scenes.title: The Magic of Modal Verbs
narration: Have you ever wondered how to show if something is possible or certain?
We use special helper words called modals to change the meaning of verbs.
Modals like can, must, and should give our sentences extra power.

scenes.title: Understanding Can, Must, Should
narration: Use can to talk about ability, like saying I can swim.
Use must when something is a rule or a strong necessity.
Use should when you are giving advice to a friend.

scenes.title: Rahul at the Park
narration: Rahul is at the park. He can climb the tall ladder easily.
He must wear his helmet while riding his bicycle.
He should drink water after playing in the sun.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Modals like can, must, and should help us express ability, rules, and advice.
Always remember that modals stay the same and never change their form.
Think about it: What is one thing you can do today that you could not do last year?

scenes.title: Spotting the Differences
narration: Look at these apples in Rohan's basket today.
How do we describe them when they are different?
We use degrees of comparison to explain size.

scenes.title: The Three Levels
narration: The positive degree is just the basic word, like big.
Comparative degree adds 'er' to compare two things, like bigger.
Superlative degree adds 'est' for three or more, like biggest.
Remember to add 'the' before the superlative word.

scenes.title: Practice with Mangoes
narration: Let us look at three delicious Alphonso mangoes.
This mango is sweet.
That one is sweeter than the first.
The last one is the sweetest of all.

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: We use three degrees to show how objects differ.
Use 'er' for two and 'est' for many.
Think about it: what is the tallest building in your city?

scenes.title: Why Punctuation Matters
narration: Have you ever seen a sentence that makes no sense at all?
Look at these words: let us eat grandma.
It sounds like we are going to have a snack of grandma!

scenes.title: The Power of Commas
narration: Now look: let us eat, grandma.
That little comma tells us we are talking to her.
Punctuation acts like traffic lights for your writing.

scenes.title: Using Marks Correctly
narration: Use a period at the end of a normal statement.
Use a question mark when you ask something.
Use an exclamation mark for excitement, like Hurray!
Anjali shouted, Look at the beautiful Taj Mahal!

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Punctuation stops confusion and gives your words the right rhythm.
Always check your sentences for periods, commas, and question marks.
Think about it: how does the meaning change if you move a comma?

scenes.title: Why Use Capital Letters?
narration: Have you ever seen a sentence that looks like a mess of lowercase letters?
Using capital letters helps us understand where a sentence starts and names important things.
Let's learn the secret rules to make your writing shine!

scenes.title: The Golden Rules
narration: Rule one: Every single sentence must start with a big capital letter.
Rule two: Always capitalize names of people like Rohan or Priya.
Rule three: Names of places like Delhi or India need a capital too.
Rule four: The word 'I' is always capitalized when you talk about yourself.

scenes.title: Example Practice
narration: Look at this sentence: my friend anjali lives in mumbai.
First, change the m in my to a capital M.
Next, capitalize Anjali because it is a person's name.
Finally, capitalize Mumbai because it is a city.
Now it reads: My friend Anjali lives in Mumbai.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember to capitalize sentence starts, names of people, places, and the word I.
Correct capitalization makes your stories clear and easy to read for everyone.
Think about it: Can you write three sentences about your school using these rules?

Other Grammar: Editing and Error Correct.topic: Other Grammar: Editing and Error Correction
Other Grammar: Editing and Error Correct.title: Fixing Your Sentences Like Magic

scenes.title: The Messy Sentence Mystery
narration: Have you ever written a story and found some tricky mistakes?
Sometimes we forget a capital letter or use the wrong word.
Let's learn how to be a grammar detective and fix these errors!

scenes.title: The Rules of the Game
narration: First, check if every sentence starts with a capital letter.
Next, make sure your subject and verb are best friends.
Finally, check if you used 'a' or 'an' correctly.
Remember, 'an' is for words starting with a, e, i, o, u.

scenes.title: Editing Rohan's Homework
narration: Rohan wrote: me and my friend goes to park.
First, 'me' should be 'my friend and I' at the start.
Then, we change 'goes' to 'go' to match the plural.
Now it reads: My friend and I go to the park.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Always check your capitals, verbs, and small words like a and an.
Editing makes your writing clear and easy for friends to read.
Think about it: Can you find one mistake in your own notebook today?

scenes.title: The Big Word Hunt
narration: Have you ever wondered why we use different words to say the same thing?
Meet Rohan who is very happy today.
Wait, can we use another word for happy?

scenes.title: What are Synonyms
narration: A synonym is a word that means the same as another word.
They help make our writing much more exciting.
Using synonyms stops our sentences from sounding boring.

scenes.title: Finding Synonyms for Rohan
narration: Rohan is happy because he won a prize.
Instead of happy, we can use the word joyful.
Or we could even say Rohan is cheerful.
See, joyful and cheerful are synonyms for happy.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Synonyms are words that have the same or similar meanings.
They add colour and style to the stories we write.
Think about it: What is another synonym for the word fast?

scenes.title: The Mystery Word Parts
narration: Have you ever seen the word unhappy and wondered why it has un at the front?
Today we are learning about prefixes, which are tiny bits added to the start of words.
Adding a prefix changes the meaning of the word completely.

scenes.title: Learning Common Prefixes
narration: The prefix un means not, like when you are unhappy or unsure.
The prefix re means to do again, like when you redo your homework.
The prefix pre means before, like a preview of a movie.

scenes.title: Prefix Practice Time
narration: Let us take the word cycle and add re to make recycle.
Now take the word heat and add pre to make preheat.
Finally, take the word tidy and add un to make untidy.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Prefixes are short sounds or letters placed at the very beginning of a word.
They help us build new words with totally new meanings.
Think about it: can you find three words in your book that start with a prefix?

scenes.title: The Mystery Of Same Sounds
narration: Have you ever noticed words that sound the same but mean different things?
Meet the homophones, words that share a sound but have their own special spelling.
Let us solve this word puzzle together today.

scenes.title: Understanding The Concept
narration: Homo means same and phone means sound.
So homophones are words that sound exactly the same, like blue and blew.
They are spelled differently and have different meanings, which makes them tricky.

scenes.title: Examples In Action
narration: Aarav has one brother, so he writes the number one.
He won the race, so he shouts that he won.
Wait, see how one and won sound alike but are totally different?
One is a number and won is a victory.

scenes.title: Recap And Practice
narration: Remember, homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.
Think about it, can you find the homophone for the word sea?

scenes.title: What are Homonyms
narration: Have you ever heard a word that sounds the same but means something else?
These sneaky words are called homonyms.
Let us see why they are so fun!

scenes.title: The Meaning of Homonyms
narration: Homonyms are words that sound identical when you say them out loud.
But, they have totally different meanings.
Knowing them helps you write better stories.

scenes.title: Example: Bat
narration: Let us look at the word bat.
First, it can be a wooden tool used in cricket.
Second, it can be a small animal that flies at night.
See how one word has two meanings?

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Homonyms sound the same but have different meanings.
They make English very exciting to learn.
Think about it: Can you find another homonym like 'park'?

scenes.title: Spotting Opposites at Home
narration: Have you ever noticed that some words are complete opposites of each other?
If I say the tea is hot, the opposite is that the ice is cold.
These pairs are called antonyms, and they make our language much more fun.

scenes.title: Learning the Rules
narration: An antonym is a word that means the direct opposite of another word.
For example, the word big is the opposite of the word small.
We use these pairs to describe things clearly in our stories and essays.
Think of it like a balance scale where words weigh in against each other.

scenes.title: Real World Examples
narration: Let us look at Rohan climbing the tall stairs to his school.
The opposite of tall is short, like the small garden fence outside.
Or think of a fast cheetah versus a slow, sleepy tortoise.
If a box is heavy, its antonym is a light feather.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Antonyms are pairs of words with opposite meanings, like happy and sad.
Using antonyms helps you describe your world with more detail and excitement.
Think about it: what is the antonym for the word bright?

scenes.title: The Mystery of New Words
narration: Have you ever wondered how we know the meaning of thousands of words?
Many English words are like trees with hidden roots beneath them.
Learning root words helps you unlock meanings of words you have never seen before.

scenes.title: What is a Root?
narration: A root word is the base part of a word that carries its main meaning.
It cannot be broken down any further into smaller parts.
When we add letters to the front or back, we change the word's shade.

scenes.title: Example: The Root 'Port'
narration: Let us look at the Latin root 'port', which means to carry.
If you 'transport' something, you carry it across a distance.
A 'portable' radio is small enough to carry with you anywhere.
Even a 'reporter' carries news from one place to another.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Root words are the base parts that hold the core meaning.
By knowing roots, you can guess the meaning of new, big words.
Think about it: Can you find three words that share the root 'act'?

scenes.title: What Are Idioms?
narration: Have you ever heard someone say it is raining cats and dogs?
Do real pets fall from the sky in India?
No, that is just a fun way to say it is raining hard.

scenes.title: Understanding Hidden Meanings
narration: An idiom is a phrase where the meaning is different from the words.
You cannot look at each word alone to understand it.
You have to learn the special group meaning together.

scenes.title: Examples In Daily Life
narration: If Rohan says piece of cake, he means it is very easy.
Like solving a simple math sum in your notebook.
If Priya says break a leg, she is wishing you good luck.
She does not actually want you to get hurt at all.

scenes.title: Recap And Practice
narration: Idioms are phrases with secret meanings that spice up our language.
Always think about the whole phrase instead of just single words.
Think about it: what do you think it means to be under the weather?

scenes.title: The Big Mystery Word
narration: Have you ever seen a word that looks like two words joined together?
Look at the word Sunflower. It is actually sun plus flower.
These special words are called compound words.

scenes.title: How They Work
narration: A compound word is two smaller words mixed to make a new one.
Think of it like building with blocks to make a bigger tower.
The new word usually has a meaning related to the two small ones.

scenes.title: Examples From Daily Life
narration: If you take rain and coat, you get a raincoat for monsoon season.
Or take play and ground to make playground where we play cricket.
And tooth plus brush makes toothbrush to keep our teeth clean.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Two small words joined together make one big compound word.
Look for them in your storybooks every single day.
Can you find a compound word in your own lunchbox today?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Word Endings
narration: Have you ever noticed how some words end with the same little pieces?
Today we will discover how these tiny endings, called suffixes, change a word completely.
Why would we add them to the end of a base word?

scenes.title: How Suffixes Work
narration: A suffix is a letter or group of letters added to the end of a base word.
It changes the word's meaning or how we use it in a sentence.
For example, adding -er to teach makes the person who does it, a teacher.
It turns a simple action into a title or a name.

scenes.title: Suffixes in Action
narration: Let's take the word care and add suffixes to it.
If we add -ful, we get careful, which means full of care.
If we add -less, we get careless, which means without any care at all.
See how the suffix completely flips the meaning of the word?

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Suffixes are endings that change the meaning of a base word.
They help us build bigger, more descriptive words from smaller ones.
Think about it: can you find a suffix in the word happiness?

scenes.title: What are Proverbs?
narration: Have you heard your grandmother say, Slow and steady wins the race?
That is a proverb, a short saying that teaches us a lesson.
They have been passed down for generations in India and beyond.

scenes.title: Understanding the Meaning
narration: Proverbs do not mean exactly what the words say.
They use pictures in our minds to share big truths.
They are like little keys that unlock ancient wisdom.

scenes.title: Example in Action
narration: Let us look at: A stitch in time saves nine.
If a shirt has one small hole, stitch it now.
If you wait, the hole grows and you need nine stitches.
This teaches us to fix problems before they get big.

scenes.title: Wrap Up and Practice
narration: Proverbs are short, wise, and teach us important life lessons.
They help us communicate our thoughts in a clever way.
Think about it: What is your favorite proverb you have heard at home?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Words
narration: Have you ever heard a word that has two different meanings?
It is like having a secret code in our language.
Let us explore how one word can play two roles.

scenes.title: Learning the Concept
narration: Some words look the same and sound the same but mean different things.
We call these multiple-meaning words.
To know the meaning, we must check how they are used in a sentence.

scenes.title: The Word Bat
narration: Think of the word bat. It can be a flying animal.
Or it can be a wooden stick used in cricket.
Look at this sentence: Rohan hit the ball with his cricket bat.
Here, bat clearly means the sports equipment.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, always look at the sentence to find the right meaning.
Words can be tricky, but you are becoming a master of English.
Think about it: can you find two meanings for the word park?

scenes.title: What is a Fiction Story
narration: Have you ever wondered why we love reading stories about talking tigers or magical kingdoms?
Fiction is a special kind of writing that comes from the author's imagination.
Even though it is made up, good fiction feels real and teaches us big lessons.

scenes.title: Key Parts of a Story
narration: Every fiction story needs characters, which are the people or animals the story is about.
The setting is where and when the story happens, like a forest or a city.
The plot is the sequence of events that builds up to the main problem.
Finally, the resolution is how the characters solve the problem at the end.

scenes.title: Example: Ravi's Lost Kite
narration: Let us imagine a story where Ravi loses his favorite kite in a tall tree.
Ravi is our character, and the park on a windy day is our setting.
Ravi climbs a nearby bench to reach the kite, which is our plot action.
He finally catches the string and flies his kite again, that is our happy resolution.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, fiction is creative writing with characters, a setting, and a plot to follow.
Reading fiction helps us build empathy and understand different points of view.
Think about it: If you were writing a story, who would your main character be?

scenes.title: The Mystery Word Hunt
narration: Have you ever found a word in a story that you did not know?
Don't worry, you can be a word detective right at home!
We use the clues around the word to guess its meaning.

scenes.title: Using Context Clues
narration: The words before and after the mystery word are called context.
Look for synonyms or descriptions that help explain the tricky word.
Sometimes the sentence tells you what the word is not.

scenes.title: A Story Example
narration: Rahul felt famished after his long football match in Delhi.
Does famished mean full or super hungry?
Because he ran all day, he must be very hungry!

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember to read the whole sentence to find hidden clues.
Context helps you become a stronger and faster reader.
Think about it: What clues would help you figure out the word 'drenched'?

scenes.title: Finding the Important News
narration: Have you ever wondered how to find the real story in a newspaper?
It is just like being a detective looking for clues in a mystery.
First, we look for the big headline at the top of the page.

scenes.title: The Five Ws
narration: Every good news story answers five special questions.
Who is the story about and what happened to them?
Where did it happen and when did it take place?
Finally, we ask why the event happened in the first place.

scenes.title: Reading a Local Story
narration: Let us look at a story about a new park in Delhi.
The headline says, New Park Opens in Dwarka.
The first sentence tells us who, what, where, and when.
It says, Families gathered today to open the green space.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Always check the headline and search for the five Ws.
Reading news helps us understand our world better every day.
Think about it: what news story would you like to write?

scenes.title: What makes a poem special?
narration: Have you ever heard words that dance like a happy song?
Poetry is a special way to paint pictures with just words.
Instead of saying 'it is raining', a poet might say 'the clouds are weeping'.

scenes.title: Key ingredients of poetry
narration: Many poems use rhyme, where word endings sound just the same.
Think of the words 'cat' and 'hat' ending with the same sound.
Rhythm is the steady beat you feel when you read aloud.
Poets also use rhythm to make the poem flow like a river.

scenes.title: Reading a poem together
narration: Let us look at a simple poem about a morning in Delhi.
The sun rises gold, over the city so bold.
The birds start to sing, what joy they will bring.
See how 'gold' and 'bold' rhyme, and 'sing' matches with 'bring'?

scenes.title: Recap and Try it
narration: Remember, poems use rhythm, rhyme, and feelings to tell stories.
Read slowly, feel the beat, and enjoy the beautiful word pictures.
Can you find a word that rhymes with 'tree' for your own poem?

scenes.title: Why read a biography
narration: Have you ever wondered how someone becomes a great leader or inventor?
A biography is a true story about a real person's life.
It tells us how they grew up and what they achieved.

scenes.title: What is inside it
narration: Authors pick important facts from the person's birth to their present day.
You will find dates, places, and big events that changed their world.
It is written by someone else, not the person themselves.

scenes.title: Example: Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam
narration: Let's look at Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam, our former President.
He was born in Rameswaram and loved studying science.
He worked hard to become the Missile Man of India.
Reading this helps us see how dreams turn into reality.

scenes.title: Recap and Explore
narration: Biographies are true stories written by others about real people.
They teach us about history and inspire us to do our best.
Think about it: If you wrote a book about your hero, who would it be?

scenes.title: What is Non-fiction?
narration: Have you ever wondered how a tiger hunts or how the moon glows?
We find these answers in special books called non-fiction.
Non-fiction books tell us about real people, places, and things.

scenes.title: Key Features to Look For
narration: These books often have a table of contents to help us find topics.
You will see labels on pictures that explain exactly what they are.
Look for a glossary at the back to understand tricky, bold words.

scenes.title: An Example in Action
narration: Imagine you are reading a book about the mighty Ganges River.
You see a photo with a caption saying Himalayan source.
You find the word tributary in bold and check the glossary.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Non-fiction is always about real facts, not made-up stories.
Use the headings and labels to learn new information quickly.
Think about it: what is one real topic you want to learn more about today?

scenes.title: Spotting The Main Idea
narration: Have you ever read a paragraph and wondered what it is truly about?
Every story has a main idea, like the main character of a play.
But how do we prove it? We look for the supporting details!

scenes.title: What Are Supporting Details
narration: Supporting details are the extra pieces of information that explain the main idea.
Think of them like the legs of a sturdy table holding up the top.
Without details, the main idea would simply fall flat on the floor.
They answer the questions: Who, what, where, when, or why.

scenes.title: A Tasty Example
narration: Let us look at a sentence: Riya made a delicious mango lassi for lunch.
Detail one: She used two fresh, sweet mangoes.
Detail two: She added a pinch of cardamom for a special scent.
Detail three: She blended it with cold yogurt and ice.

scenes.title: Wrapping It All Up
narration: Main ideas give the topic, while supporting details give the proof.
Always look for facts that tell you more about the main subject.
Can you find three details in your favorite book today?

scenes.title: The Big Mystery
narration: Have you ever read a paragraph and wondered what it was really about?
Think of a paragraph like a delicious vegetable curry.
The main idea is the main ingredient that makes it taste like curry.

scenes.title: What is the Main Idea?
narration: The main idea is the most important point the author wants you to know.
It tells you the big picture of what you are reading.
All other sentences are just details that support that one big idea.

scenes.title: Let's Practice Together
narration: Anish loves playing cricket, football, and badminton every single evening.
These sports keep Anish very active and healthy after his long school day.
The main idea is: Anish enjoys playing many sports to stay healthy.

scenes.title: Wrap Up and Review
narration: Remember, the main idea is the heart of the paragraph.
Look at the topic sentence, usually found at the very start.
Think about it: What is the main idea of your favorite storybook?

scenes.title: The Mystery Of Reading
narration: Have you ever wondered why your friend is wearing a raincoat?
You guess it is raining even without looking outside.
In stories, authors leave hidden clues for us too.

scenes.title: How To Make Inferences
narration: An inference is like being a story detective.
You combine what the text says with what you already know.
Think: Text clues plus my knowledge equals my inference.

scenes.title: Solving A Story Mystery
narration: Imagine Rohan drops his ice cream and starts to cry.
The text does not say he is sad, but we know why.
We infer Rohan is sad because he lost his treat.
Good readers use these clues to understand feelings.

scenes.title: Wrap Up And Think
narration: Remember, check the text and use your own brain.
Inference helps you read between the lines easily.
Think about it: What clues show a character is happy?

scenes.title: What Happens Next?
narration: Have you ever wondered how a story ends before you finish reading?
Prediction is like being a detective using clues to guess the future.
It helps us understand the story better as we read along.

scenes.title: Finding The Clues
narration: First, look at the book cover and the title for hints.
Next, think about what you already know about the world.
Then, check how the characters are acting in the scene.
These pieces fit together to help you make a smart guess.

scenes.title: A Story Example
narration: Let us read: Rahul ran to the dark clouds with his umbrella.
I see dark clouds, so I think it will rain soon.
Rahul has an umbrella, which matches my guess about the rain.
My prediction was correct because I used the text clues.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Remember, predictions use clues and your own knowledge to guess.
It is okay if your guess changes as you read more.
Think about it: what clue helps you predict the next page?

scenes.title: What Is The Goal?
narration: Have you ever wondered why authors write books like the ones in your school library?
Every piece of writing has a reason, or a purpose, for being created.
Authors usually write to persuade, inform, or entertain us.

scenes.title: Understanding The Three Reasons
narration: When an author wants to inform, they share true facts about things like history.
When they persuade, they try to convince you to believe something or take action.
When they entertain, they write stories just for your enjoyment and fun.

scenes.title: Let Us Check Examples
narration: Imagine an article titled All About Tigers in India. Its purpose is to inform.
What if you read a poster that says Eat More Fruits? That is to persuade.
And a funny tale about a clever rabbit? That is written to entertain.

scenes.title: Recap And Think
narration: Remember, authors write to inform with facts, persuade with opinions, or entertain with stories.
Always look for clues in the text to figure out why the author wrote it.
Think about it: What was the purpose of the last book you read at home?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Events
narration: Have you ever wondered why your umbrella pops up when it rains?
In stories, every action has a reason behind it.
We call these causes and effects.

scenes.title: Defining the Key Concepts
narration: The cause is why something happens.
The effect is what happens because of that.
Think of it like a chain reaction in your book.

scenes.title: A Sunny Day Example
narration: Rohan forgot his water bottle at home today.
So, Rohan felt very thirsty during playtime.
Because he forgot it, he had to buy juice.

scenes.title: Quick Recap and Challenge
narration: Cause is the why, and effect is the result.
Look for signal words like because, so, and therefore.
Think about it: What is the effect if you study for your test?

scenes.title: What is a Fact?
narration: Do you prefer mangoes or apples for your lunch box?
A fact is something that can be proven true by anyone.
For example, India is a country in Asia.

scenes.title: What is an Opinion?
narration: An opinion is how someone feels about something.
It is not always true for everyone else.
Saying that cricket is the best game is an opinion.

scenes.title: Spotting the Difference
narration: Rohan says, The Taj Mahal is in Agra. That is a fact.
Rohan also says, The Taj Mahal is beautiful. That is his opinion.
Look for words like best, beautiful, or fun to spot opinions.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Facts are proven, and opinions are feelings.
Always check if you can prove it with evidence.
Think about it: Is 'Chocolate ice cream is yummy' a fact or opinion?

scenes.title: What Are You Reading Today
narration: Have you ever wondered how a story about a jungle and a city are different?
When we compare, we look for ways two things are the same.
When we contrast, we look for ways they are different.

scenes.title: Learning the Key Words
narration: Look for words like both, also, or similar to find how things match.
Use words like but, unlike, or however to show how they change.
Using these words helps you organize your thoughts while you read.

scenes.title: Comparing Two Famous Stories
narration: Think of a story about a tiger and a story about a pet cat.
Both animals have whiskers and sharp claws, which is a similarity.
But, a tiger lives in the wild, unlike the cat living at home.

scenes.title: Recap and Your Turn
narration: Comparing finds the match, while contrasting finds the difference.
Using key words helps you understand any story you read.
Can you compare and contrast your favorite book with your favorite movie?

scenes.title: The Big Essay Hook
narration: Have you ever wanted to tell a great story but did not know where to start?
Writing an essay is just like building a tall tower with blocks.
It needs a strong base to hold everything together.

scenes.title: Three Main Parts
narration: First, the Introduction introduces your main topic clearly.
Second, the Body paragraphs give cool facts and details.
Finally, the Conclusion wraps it all up neatly.

scenes.title: Writing About My School
narration: Let us write about our school playground in Delhi.
Start with: My school has a big green playground.
Next, add details like the slide and the swing set.
End with: I love playing there every single day.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Remember, an essay needs an introduction, body, and conclusion.
Use simple words and check your spelling carefully.
Think about it: What is one thing you would love to write an essay about today?

scenes.title: The Big Idea
narration: Have you ever told a friend about a long movie in just a few sentences?
That is exactly what a summary is: picking the most important parts to share.
Summarizing helps us remember stories and share ideas quickly with others.

scenes.title: How to Summarize
narration: First, read the whole text carefully and look for the main character.
Next, identify the biggest problem or the main goal of the story.
Finally, find out how the story ends and leave out small, unimportant details.

scenes.title: A Quick Example
narration: Imagine a story about Rohan, who loses his cricket bat before a big match.
He searches everywhere, asks his friends, and finally finds it under the sofa.
Rohan reaches the match just in time and hits a winning six!
A summary is: Rohan lost his cricket bat but found it in time to win the match.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, a summary uses your own words and captures the most important facts.
Always focus on the main character, the main problem, and the final outcome.
Think about it: Can you summarize your favorite storybook in just three sentences?

scenes.title: The Hook
narration: Have you ever tried to tell a story but it turned into a big jumble?
Writing is just like building a Lego set, you need to follow a plan.
Today we will learn how to write a perfect, clear paragraph.

scenes.title: The Idea
narration: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea.
First, the topic sentence tells the reader what you are writing about.
Next, supporting sentences give facts or details to explain your idea.
Finally, the concluding sentence wraps everything up with a final thought.

scenes.title: An Example
narration: Let us write about our favorite fruit, the mango.
Topic: The mango is the most delicious fruit in India.
Details: It is sweet, juicy, and grows in summer heat.
Conclusion: Everyone loves eating fresh mangoes during the holidays.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember, start with a main idea, add facts, and finish strong.
Keep your sentences focused so your reader can follow along easily.
Think about it: What is one topic you could write a paragraph about today?

scenes.title: What Are Mystery Words?
narration: Have you ever been reading a story and bumped into a word you did not know?
Don't worry! You do not always need a dictionary to find the meaning.
We can look for clues hidden right inside the sentence to help us understand.

scenes.title: Using Sentence Clues
narration: First, look at the other words surrounding the mystery word.
Think about what the whole sentence is trying to tell you.
These clues are like detective breadcrumbs leading you to the answer.

scenes.title: Solving a Story Puzzle
narration: Rohan felt famished after his long cricket match, so he ate a huge plate of biryani.
The word is famished. What clues tell us what it means?
He ate a huge plate of food, so famished must mean very hungry.

scenes.title: Reviewing Our Detective Skills
narration: Remember, check the words before and after the mystery word for hints.
Use your brain to guess the meaning, then see if it fits the story.
Think about it: can you find a new word today and use context clues to define it?

scenes.title: The Hook: Start A Tale
narration: Have you ever wanted to write a story as exciting as your favorite adventure book?
Every great story starts with just one small, creative idea.
Let us learn how to build a story step by step.

scenes.title: The Ingredients of Stories
narration: First, every story needs a character, like Kabir who loves to explore.
Next, give them a setting, like a busy market in Delhi.
Finally, add a plot, which is the problem the hero must solve.

scenes.title: Example: Kabir's Lost Kite
narration: Kabir is in the park, and his colorful kite gets stuck in a tall tree.
He asks his friend Ananya to help him reach it with a long stick.
They work together and safely get the kite down, feeling very happy.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, a good story needs a character, a place, and an exciting problem.
Keep your sentences clear and use descriptive words to paint a picture.
Think about it: What is the first sentence of your very own adventure story?

scenes.title: The Magic of Ideas
narration: Have you ever wanted to write a story that makes your friends giggle or gasp?
Creative writing is like painting a picture, but using words instead of colours.
Let us learn how to turn a simple spark into an amazing adventure.

scenes.title: Building Your Story World
narration: First, choose a main character, like Rohan who discovers a secret map in his bag.
Second, set the scene, maybe in a busy market in Delhi or a quiet forest.
Third, add a problem, like finding a locked chest that needs a special key.
Finally, show how they solve it to make your reader happy.

scenes.title: Showing, Not Just Telling
narration: Instead of saying Rohan was scared, try showing it through his actions.
Write: Rohan shook, his teeth chattered, and he hid behind a big tree.
Using descriptive words makes your reader feel like they are right there with him.

scenes.title: Recap and Your Turn
narration: Remember, every great story needs a character, a place, and a small problem.
Use your senses to show what is happening so your readers can imagine it.
Think about it: If you found a magic key in your school bag, where would it lead?

scenes.title: The Hook: Start A Story
narration: Have you ever wanted to write a story about a dragon in Mumbai?
Every great story needs a beginning, a middle, and an end.
Let's learn how to build your own exciting narrative today!

scenes.title: The Building Blocks
narration: First, introduce your characters and the setting in the beginning.
Next, the middle shows a problem that needs to be solved.
Finally, the end shows how the characters fixed it.

scenes.title: Let's Write Together
narration: Imagine Rohan finds a shiny gold coin at the park.
He realizes the coin is magic and starts to glow.
Rohan uses the coin to help his friends finish their homework.

scenes.title: Recap And Think
narration: Remember, every story needs characters, a problem, and a solution.
Use descriptive words to make your story come alive for readers.
Think about it: What is one problem your hero could face tomorrow?

scenes.title: The Magic of Descriptive Words
narration: Have you ever read a story and felt like you were actually inside it?
That happens when writers use descriptive words to paint a picture in your mind.
Instead of saying the dog is big, you can describe how it looks and acts.

scenes.title: Choosing Your Sensory Details
narration: To describe well, use your five senses to tell us what you see, hear, or feel.
Use adjectives like shiny, soft, or loud to make your sentences pop.
Strong verbs tell us exactly how something moves or happens.

scenes.title: Describing a Busy Indian Market
narration: Let's describe a market. Don't just say it is busy.
Try: The golden marigolds glowed brightly under the warm sun.
Or: The spicy aroma of fresh samosas filled the cool morning air.
See how those words help you smell and see the scene?

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Descriptive writing uses senses, adjectives, and strong verbs to build a scene.
It turns a simple sentence into a vibrant, exciting story for your reader.
Think about it: How would you describe your favourite meal to a friend?

scenes.title: What is a Diary Entry
narration: Have you ever wanted to talk to a secret friend about your day?
A diary entry is like a letter you write only to yourself.
It helps you remember fun events like your trip to Mysore Palace.

scenes.title: The Key Ingredients
narration: Always start with the date so you know when it happened.
Use a friendly greeting like Dear Diary to start your page.
Since it is about you, use I, me, and my.
Write in the past tense because the day is already over.

scenes.title: An Example Entry
narration: Imagine today you visited the park and ate a yummy samosa.
You could write, Today I went to the park.
Then add, I enjoyed a spicy samosa with my friend.
End by signing your name at the bottom of the page.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Remember, use the date, a greeting, and your own feelings.
Keep your diary in a safe place to protect your secrets.
Think about it: What is the most exciting thing that happened to you today?

scenes.title: Sending Messages Online
narration: Have you ever wondered how your teacher receives your digital homework so fast?
It is all thanks to a quick, friendly tool called an email.
Emails are like letters, but they travel across the internet in a blink!

scenes.title: Parts of an Email
narration: First, you need a clear Subject line so the reader knows the topic.
Always start with a polite greeting like Dear Teacher or Dear Rohan.
Write your message clearly, then finish with a sign-off like Best regards.
Finally, add your name at the bottom so they know it is you.

scenes.title: Writing a Sample Email
narration: Imagine you are writing to your teacher, Ms. Gupta, about your history project.
Subject: My History Project. Dear Ms. Gupta, here is my project about the Taj Mahal.
Best regards, Aryan. Always check your spelling before clicking that blue send button.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Remember: clear subjects, polite greetings, and always sign your name.
Emails are a professional way to share information with friends and teachers.
Think about it: who would you like to email today to share some good news?

scenes.title: The Hook: Sending a Message
narration: Have you ever needed to write a letter to your school principal about a special request?
We do not use casual chat words like hey or lol when writing to officials.
Instead, we use a formal tone to be polite and clear. Shall we learn how?

scenes.title: The Parts of a Letter
narration: First, write your address and the date at the very top on the left side.
Next, write the receiver's name or title and their official address below that.
Always include a clear subject line so the reader knows exactly what it is about.
Start with a polite greeting like Dear Sir or Dear Madam.

scenes.title: Writing the Body Example
narration: Let us ask for a leave of absence for a cousin's wedding in Jaipur.
State your reason clearly in the first paragraph.
Then, add the specific dates you will be away.
End with a formal sign-off like Yours faithfully and your full name.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Remember, keep it polite, clear, and structured correctly.
Check your spelling and punctuation before you send it off.
Think about it: Who is the next person you need to write a formal letter to?

scenes.title: A Surprise in the Post
narration: Have you ever received a handwritten letter in the post from a friend?
It feels special, right? Today, let's learn how to write one!
Informal letters are notes we write to people we know well.

scenes.title: The Structure of a Letter
narration: First, write your address and the date in the top right corner.
Next, start with a friendly greeting like Dear Ravi or Dear Meera.
The main part is your message, written in clear, simple paragraphs.
Finally, add a warm closing like With love or Best wishes.

scenes.title: Writing to Arjun
narration: Let us write to Arjun about your fun summer vacation in Shimla.
Start with Dear Arjun, and tell him about the cold weather.
Mention the delicious apples you ate from the local market.
End with With love, and sign your name at the bottom.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember to include your address, a greeting, your message, and a closing.
Keep your tone casual and warm, just like talking to a friend.
Think about it: who would you like to surprise with a letter today?

scenes.title: What is a Report?
narration: Have you ever wanted to tell your class about something cool you discovered?
A report is a special way to share facts clearly.
It helps others learn about a topic just like you did.

scenes.title: The Report Plan
narration: Every good report needs a catchy title at the top.
Next, write an introduction to say what the report is about.
Then, use subheadings to group your interesting facts.
Finally, add a conclusion to summarize your main points.

scenes.title: Writing About Tigers
narration: Let's write a report about the Royal Bengal Tiger.
We start with a title like: The Majestic Bengal Tiger.
Under Habitat, we say they live in the Sundarbans.
Under Diet, we write they hunt deer and wild boar.
In the conclusion, we explain why we must protect them.

scenes.title: Wrap Up and Review
narration: Remember, keep your sentences short and stick to facts.
Always check your spelling and your punctuation too.
Now, what topic would you like to write a report about today?

scenes.title: Looking at the Picture
narration: Have you ever seen a picture and wanted to tell a story about it?
A picture composition is just writing down what you see and what you imagine.
Let us learn how to turn a simple image into a great story.

scenes.title: The Three Simple Steps
narration: First, look at the background and the setting of the picture.
Second, describe the characters and what they are doing.
Third, add your own creative ideas about what happens next.

scenes.title: Example: A Day at the Park
narration: Imagine a park in Delhi with children playing near a slide.
We write, The sun is bright, and Rohan is sliding down fast.
We use adjectives, like saying the green grass is soft.
Finally, we say they feel happy playing together today.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember to describe the place, the characters, and the action.
Use interesting words to make your reader see what you see.
Think about it: what story would you write about a rainy day?

scenes.title: The Mystery Of The Story
narration: Have you ever tried to tell a friend about a long movie in just one minute?
That is what we call a summary, and it is a super useful skill.
A summary tells the main points without all the extra, tiny details.

scenes.title: How To Write A Summary
narration: First, read the whole story carefully so you understand what happens.
Next, pick out the important characters and the big events.
Finally, write those points in your own words, keeping it very short.
Remember, do not include every single thing that the characters said.

scenes.title: Let's Practice Together
narration: Imagine a story about Rohan who lost his kite in a big banyan tree.
He climbed up, slipped, but luckily caught a branch to stay safe.
A summary would be: Rohan climbed a tree to get his kite and stayed safe.

scenes.title: Wrap Up And Think
narration: So, a good summary is short, uses your own words, and shows the main idea.
It helps you remember what you read and explain it to others easily.
Think about it: what is the most important thing that happened in your favorite book today?

scenes.title: The First Meeting
narration: Have you ever met someone new and felt shy about what to say?
Introducing yourself is a superpower that helps you make new friends easily.
Let us learn how to speak clearly and confidently when you meet people.

scenes.title: The Three Magic Steps
narration: Step one is your greeting, like saying Hello or Good Morning.
Step two is stating your name clearly so everyone can hear you.
Step three is sharing one fun fact about yourself, like your favorite hobby.

scenes.title: An Example in Action
narration: Imagine you are Rohan meeting a new classmate at school.
You say: Hello, my name is Rohan, and I love playing cricket.
Remember to smile and look at the person while you are speaking.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: To introduce yourself, always greet, state your name, and share a hobby.
Speaking clearly makes you sound friendly and ready to chat.
Think about it: What is one fun fact you would tell a new friend?

scenes.title: The Magic Of Good Listening
narration: Have you ever tried talking while someone else is looking at their phone?
It makes us feel like our words do not matter.
What if we could make every conversation feel like a fun game of catch?

scenes.title: Three Rules For Great Talk
narration: First, make eye contact to show you are truly listening.
Second, wait for the other person to finish before you start.
Third, ask a question to show you want to know more.

scenes.title: A Chat At The Park
narration: Imagine Rohan tells Priya, I love playing cricket.
Priya listens, then asks, Who is your favorite player?
Now, the conversation flows because Priya was a good listener.

scenes.title: Recap And Think
narration: Listen well, wait your turn, and ask curious questions.
Conversations are bridges that connect us to each other.
Think about it: who is one person you will listen to today?

scenes.title: The Big School Assembly
narration: Have you ever felt nervous before speaking in front of your whole class?
Giving a presentation is just like telling a great story to your friends.
Let us learn how to speak clearly and keep everyone interested.

scenes.title: Preparing Your Talk
narration: First, pick a topic you truly love, like the history of Delhi.
Write down your main points on small cue cards to help you remember.
Practice in front of a mirror or with your family at home.
Remember to speak slowly so everyone can understand your words.

scenes.title: During Your Presentation
narration: Stand tall, look at your friends, and give a friendly smile.
Use a clear voice so that the person in the back can hear.
If you make a mistake, just smile and keep going.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember to prepare well, speak slowly, and always make eye contact.
Presenting is a skill that gets easier every single time.
Think about it: What topic would you love to teach your class tomorrow?

scenes.title: The Hook
narration: Have you ever wondered why some stories keep us listening until the very end?
Today, we will learn how to tell a great story just like a professional writer.
Imagine you are telling your friends about a funny day at the park.

scenes.title: The Idea
narration: A good story needs a clear beginning to introduce your characters and setting.
Next, include a middle part where something exciting or tricky happens.
Finally, the ending shares how the problem was solved and how everyone feels.
Use descriptive words to help your listeners picture the world you create.

scenes.title: Example Story
narration: Let us tell a story about Rahul finding a lost kite in Delhi.
Rahul looked up, saw the bright red kite stuck high in a tree.
He climbed carefully, reached out, and finally grabbed the kite safely.
He flew it high above the park, feeling proud and very happy.

scenes.title: Recap
narration: Remember, a great story has a beginning, a middle, and a happy ending.
Use your voice to show excitement and help your friends hear the magic.
Think about it: what is the most exciting story you can tell today?

Speaking and Listening: Asking and Answe.topic: Speaking and Listening: Asking and Answering Questions
Speaking and Listening: Asking and Answe.title: Mastering the Art of Questions

scenes.title: The Curious Detective
narration: Have you ever wondered how to learn more about everything around you?
When you want to know something, you just need to ask a good question.
Let us learn how to be great listeners and expert question askers today.

scenes.title: The Question Starters
narration: Use words like Who, What, Where, When, Why, and How to start.
Use Who to ask about people, like your friend Rohan or your teacher.
Use Where to find out about places, like the park or the library.
Use Why to understand the reason behind something that happened.

scenes.title: Practicing with Priya
narration: Priya shows you her new bicycle bought for five thousand rupees.
You can ask, What color is your bicycle?
Or you can ask, How fast can you ride it?
Listen carefully to her answer so you can reply with something interesting.

scenes.title: Recap and Reflect
narration: Remember to use your question starters to get the information you need.
Always listen to the full answer before you ask your next question.
Think about it: What is one question you will ask your friend tomorrow?

scenes.title: Why Opinions Matter
narration: Have you ever disagreed about which game to play during recess?
Sharing what you think is called an opinion.
It is how we tell others what we feel or believe.

scenes.title: Using Polite Phrases
narration: Always start by saying I think or in my opinion.
These words show you are ready to share respectfully.
Always listen carefully while others share their views too.

scenes.title: Giving Your Reason
narration: Imagine we are deciding if mangoes are the best fruit.
You could say I think mangoes are best because they are sweet.
Adding because makes your opinion much stronger and clearer.
Even if your friend likes apples, you both have valid points.

scenes.title: Recap And Practice
narration: Remember to use polite phrases and explain your reasons.
Listening to others helps us learn new things every day.
What is one opinion you have about your favorite school subject?

scenes.title: Why Instructions Matter
narration: Have you ever tried to explain a game to a friend but they got confused?
Giving instructions is like building a bridge of words between you and your listener.
Today we will learn how to give clear steps for any task.

scenes.title: The Golden Rules
narration: First, always start with a polite opening like, Please help me.
Second, use transition words like first, next, and finally.
Third, keep your sentences short and direct.
Lastly, check if your listener understands by asking, Does that make sense?

scenes.title: Example: Making Nimbu Pani
narration: Let us instruct a friend to make fresh Nimbu Pani.
First, squeeze half a lemon into a glass of water.
Next, add one spoon of sugar and a pinch of salt.
Finally, stir the drink well with a spoon until it dissolves.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember to be polite, use order words, and keep it simple.
Clear instructions help everyone complete tasks safely and quickly.
Think about it: What instructions would you give to teach someone to tie their shoes?

scenes.title: Why Listen Carefully
narration: Have you ever missed a cool instruction because you were busy daydreaming?
Listening is more than hearing sounds; it is understanding the speaker's true meaning.
Let us learn to catch every detail like a detective solving a mystery.

scenes.title: The Three Magic Steps
narration: First, focus your eyes on the person speaking to you.
Next, ignore distractions like your toys or a buzzing mobile phone.
Finally, wait until they finish before you think of your reply.
These steps help you understand every single word clearly.

scenes.title: Listening to Rohan
narration: Rohan says, Please bring a red pen and an eraser to class.
A good listener hears red pen, not just any pen.
You remember the eraser too because you were fully listening.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Always keep eye contact and avoid distractions while listening.
Wait for the speaker to finish before asking your questions.
Think about it: Can you listen to a story today and retell it to a friend?
